q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, collisions of gas molecules with one another and with the walls of the container are:
o: Partly elastic, with some energy lost as heat
x: KMT assumes all collisions are perfectly elastic: the total kinetic energy of the colliding molecules is the same before and after a collision. Energy may pass from one molecule to another, but none is lost.

q: In FSc chemistry, the standard temperature used in STP is:
x: STP means standard temperature, 0 °C or 273 K, and standard pressure, 1 atm. 298 K (25 °C) is the standard temperature used for thermochemical data, not for STP.

q: Boyle's law states that, for a given mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is:
o: Directly proportional to the absolute temperature
x: Boyle's law: at constant temperature V ∝ 1/P, so PV = constant. Direct proportionality of volume to absolute temperature is Charles's law.

q: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at:
x: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is negligible, and at high temperature they move so fast that attractions hardly matter. High pressure and low temperature cause the largest deviations.

q: Which of the following is NOT a postulate of the kinetic molecular theory of gases?
o: Gas molecules attract one another strongly at all temperatures
The actual volume of gas molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container
Gas molecules move randomly in straight lines between collisions
The average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature
x: KMT assumes there are no forces of attraction or repulsion between gas molecules. The other three statements are standard postulates.

q: Standard pressure, as used in STP, is:
x: Standard pressure is 1 atmosphere, the pressure that supports a 760 mm column of mercury. 76 cm Hg is the same thing, but 76 mm Hg is ten times too small.

q: A gas occupies 6 dm³ at 2 atm. What will its volume be at 3 atm if the temperature does not change?
x: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ gives V₂ = (2 × 6)/3 = 4 dm³. Using the pressure ratio upside down gives the wrong answer 9 dm³; higher pressure must give a smaller volume.

q: Deviations of real gases from ideal behaviour show that two postulates of the kinetic molecular theory are faulty. These two are:
o: Perfectly elastic collisions and random motion
Negligible volume of molecules and no attractive forces between them
Random motion and kinetic energy proportional to temperature
Pressure due to wall collisions and perfectly elastic collisions
x: Real gas molecules do have a definite volume and do attract each other. These two assumptions fail at high pressure and low temperature, and van der Waals corrected both.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the pressure of a gas is caused by:
o: The weight of the molecules pressing on the bottom
Collisions of the molecules with the walls of the container
Vibration of the molecules about fixed positions
x: Each molecule that strikes a wall exerts a force on it; the total force per unit area from countless collisions is the gas pressure. KMT assumes no attractive forces, and gas molecules do not vibrate about fixed positions as in solids.

q: The volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at STP is:
x: One mole of any ideal gas at 0 °C and 1 atm occupies 22.414 dm³ (about 22.4 dm³). About 24 dm³ is the molar volume at room temperature, not at STP.

q: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 600 mm Hg. What pressure is needed to compress it to 100 cm³ at constant temperature?
x: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = (600 × 250)/100 = 1500 mm Hg. Inverting the volume ratio gives 240 mm Hg, but compressing a gas needs a higher pressure, not a lower one.

q: In the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, the constant a corrects for:
o: The volume of the gas molecules themselves
The mass of the gas molecules
Attractive forces between the gas molecules
x: The term an²/V² is the pressure correction: attractions reduce the force of molecules hitting the walls, so a measures the strength of intermolecular attraction. The constant b corrects for molecular volume.

q: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is directly proportional to its:
x: KMT states that average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature. It cannot be proportional to the Celsius temperature, since molecules still have kinetic energy at 0 °C.

q: Standard pressure expressed in pascals is:
x: 1 atm = 101325 Pa (about 101.3 kPa). 760 is the value in mm Hg or torr, not in pascals; 1013.25 is the value in hectopascals (millibars).

q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure (y-axis) against volume (x-axis) is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the volume axis
A straight line rising with volume
A curve (hyperbola) falling as volume increases
x: Since PV = constant, P falls as V rises along a hyperbola. A straight line through the origin is obtained when P is plotted against 1/V instead.

q: In the van der Waals equation, the constant b represents:
o: The excluded volume, due to the finite size of the molecules
The strength of attraction between molecules
The pressure correction for wall collisions
The average kinetic energy of the molecules
x: b is the effective (excluded) volume per mole of molecules, so the free space for movement is V − nb. It is larger than the actual volume of the molecules themselves.

q: In the kinetic gas equation PV = ⅓ mNc̄², the symbol N stands for:
o: The number of moles of the gas
The number of molecules in the gas
The number of collisions per second
The number of molecules in one mole only
x: In PV = ⅓ mNc̄², m is the mass of one molecule, N is the number of molecules present and c̄² is the mean square velocity. N is not the number of moles and is not fixed at Avogadro's number.

q: The density of methane, CH₄, at STP is approximately: (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: Density = molar mass / molar volume = 16/22.4 ≈ 0.71 g dm⁻³. Dividing the other way round (22.4/16) gives the wrong value 1.40.

q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure against 1/V is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the 1/V axis
A curve that rises and then falls
x: Boyle's law gives P = k × (1/V), which is the equation of a straight line through the origin with slope k. The hyperbola is obtained for P against V.

q: For an ideal gas, the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT is:
o: Equal to 1 at all pressures and temperatures
x: An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT exactly, so PV/nRT = 1 under all conditions. A value of Z different from 1 measures how far a real gas deviates.

q: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. At constant pressure, its volume at 127 °C will be:
x: Charles's law needs kelvin: V₂ = 300 × (127 + 273)/(27 + 273) = 300 × 400/300 = 400 cm³. Using the Celsius values (300 × 127/27) gives about 1411 cm³; inverting the ratio gives 225 cm³.

q: Under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, the ratio of the rate of diffusion of H₂ to that of O₂ is: (H = 1, O = 16)
x: By Graham's law, rate ∝ 1/√M, so rate(H₂)/rate(O₂) = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. Forgetting the square root gives 16 : 1, and inverting the masses gives 1 : 4.

q: Under identical conditions, 100 cm³ of methane (CH₄) effuses through a small hole in 20 s, while 100 cm³ of gas X takes 40 s. The molar mass of X is: (C = 12, H = 1)
x: For equal volumes, time ∝ √M, so t(X)/t(CH₄) = √(M/16) = 40/20 = 2; squaring, M = 4 × 16 = 64 g mol⁻¹ (for example SO₂). Forgetting to square gives 32 g mol⁻¹; treating time as proportional to rate gives 4 g mol⁻¹.

q: A vessel contains 2 g of H₂ and 16 g of O₂ at a total pressure of 3 atm. The partial pressure of O₂ is: (H = 1, O = 16)
x: Moles: H₂ = 1, O₂ = 0.5, total 1.5; mole fraction of O₂ = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3, so p(O₂) = 3 × 1/3 = 1 atm. Using the mass fraction (16/18) gives 2.67 atm; 2 atm is the partial pressure of H₂.

q: By extending Charles's law, the volume of an ideal gas at constant pressure would in theory become zero at:
x: Volume falls by 1/273.15 of its 0 °C value for each degree of cooling, so it would reach zero at −273.15 °C, which is absolute zero (0 K). Choosing 0 °C confuses the Celsius zero with absolute zero.

q: What volume is occupied by 2 mol of an ideal gas at 27 °C and 2 atm? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: V = nRT/P = 2 × 0.0821 × 300/2 = 24.6 dm³. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives 2.22 dm³; forgetting to divide by the pressure gives 49.3 dm³.

q: A gas has a density of 2.5 g dm⁻³ at 273 K and 2 atm. Its molar mass is: (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 273 = 22.4)
x: From PM = dRT, M = dRT/P = 2.5 × 22.4/2 = 28 g mol⁻¹. Forgetting to divide by P (as if it were at 1 atm) gives 56 g mol⁻¹.

q: 8.8 g of CO₂ is placed in an 8.21 dm³ vessel at 227 °C. The pressure of the gas is: (C = 12, O = 16; R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: n = 8.8/44 = 0.2 mol and T = 227 + 273 = 500 K, so P = nRT/V = 0.2 × 0.0821 × 500/8.21 = 1.0 atm. Using 227 instead of 500 K gives about 0.45 atm; using the mass 8.8 as if it were moles gives 44 atm.

q: For a fixed ideal gas, which change doubles its density?
o: Doubling the pressure at constant temperature
Doubling the kelvin temperature at constant pressure
Doubling both the pressure and the kelvin temperature
Halving the pressure at constant temperature
x: Density d = PM/RT, so d ∝ P/T. Doubling P at constant T doubles d; doubling T halves d; doubling both leaves d unchanged. Thinking that heating makes a gas denser is the common slip.

q: One mole of an ideal gas is at 27 °C and a pressure of 83.14 kPa. Its volume is: (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: With SI units, V = nRT/P = 1 × 8.314 × 300/83140 Pa = 0.030 m³ = 30 dm³ (1 m³ = 1000 dm³). Leaving the answer as 0.030 and labelling it dm³ is the unit slip; using 27 instead of 300 K gives 2.7 dm³.

q: Compared with O₂ molecules at the same temperature, H₂ molecules have: (H = 1, O = 16)
o: The same average kinetic energy and sixteen times the root-mean-square speed
The same average kinetic energy and four times the root-mean-square speed
Sixteen times the average kinetic energy and the same root-mean-square speed
Four times the average kinetic energy and four times the root-mean-square speed
x: Average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so it is the same. Since ½mc² is equal, c ∝ 1/√m and c(H₂)/c(O₂) = √(32/2) = 4. Forgetting the square root gives sixteen times.

q: The temperature of a gas is raised from 27 °C to 927 °C. The root-mean-square speed of its molecules becomes:
x: Root-mean-square speed ∝ √T in kelvin: T rises from 300 K to 1200 K, four times, so the speed doubles. Forgetting the square root gives 4 times; using Celsius values (927/27 ≈ 34) gives the larger options.

q: According to kinetic molecular theory, when a gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature, its pressure doubles because the molecules:
o: Move faster and hit the walls harder
Become larger and fill more of the container
Hit each unit area of the walls more often, with the same average speed
x: At constant temperature the average kinetic energy and speed do not change; in half the volume each molecule reaches the walls twice as often, so the force per unit area doubles. Saying the molecules move faster would need a rise in temperature.

q: According to kinetic molecular theory, between collisions the molecules of a gas move:
o: In straight lines at constant speed, in random directions
In circular paths around the centre of the container
In zigzag paths caused by attraction to other molecules
Only towards the walls of the container
x: Since no forces act between molecules except during collisions, each molecule travels in a straight line until it hits another molecule or a wall, and the directions are random. The zigzag path comes from many collisions, not from attraction between molecules.

q: Kinetic theory gives the average translational kinetic energy of one mole of an ideal gas as (3/2)RT. For one mole at 300 K this energy is: (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: E = 1.5 × 8.314 × 300 = 3741 J ≈ 3.74 kJ. Using RT alone (forgetting the factor 3/2) gives 2.49 kJ.

q: At a moderate pressure, the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT of a real gas is found to be less than 1. This shows that:
o: The volume of the molecules is important, so the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas
The gas is behaving exactly as an ideal gas
Attractive forces between the molecules are important, so the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas
x: Attractions pull molecules together and lower the pressure on the walls, so PV is smaller than nRT and Z < 1. When the molecules' own volume dominates, usually at very high pressure, Z > 1, which is the tempting reversal.

q: Which gas has the largest value of the van der Waals constant a?
x: The constant a measures intermolecular attraction. NH₃ is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, so its attractions are much stronger than the weak London forces in He, H₂ and N₂, which is also why it is the most easily liquefied. Choosing N₂ because it is the heaviest molecule overlooks polarity.

q: In Linde's method of liquefying air, the compressed gas cools when it expands through a fine nozzle because its molecules:
o: Gain kinetic energy as they move apart
Use part of their kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular attractions as they move apart
x: On expansion the molecules move apart against their mutual attractions; the work done comes from their kinetic energy, so the temperature falls (the Joule–Thomson effect). Repeating the cycle cools the gas until it liquefies. Thinking expansion raises kinetic energy reverses the effect.

q: Plasma, sometimes called the fourth state of matter, differs from an ordinary gas because it:
o: Consists only of neutral molecules at very low temperature
Contains free electrons and positive ions, so it conducts electricity
Has a fixed shape and volume
Carries an overall large positive charge
x: Plasma is an ionised gas of free electrons, positive ions and some neutral particles, formed at very high temperature or in electric discharges; the charged particles let it conduct electricity. It is electrically neutral overall, so calling it positively charged is the slip.

q: Critical temperatures: CO₂ 304 K, O₂ 155 K, N₂ 126 K, H₂ 33 K. At 25 °C, which of these gases can be liquefied by applying pressure alone?
x: A gas can be liquefied by pressure only below its critical temperature. 25 °C = 298 K, which is below 304 K for CO₂ but above the critical temperatures of O₂, N₂ and H₂. Thinking a low critical temperature makes liquefaction easier gives the reversed choices.
